verses.verse:
कम्पनम् स्वर एकस्मिन् वैपरीत्यं स्वरद्वये।
स्वरत्रते तु लंघः स्यात् संचारस्तु चतुष्टये।१०१।
verses.text: On one note there is kampana (shake); on two notes, vaiparītya (reversal); on three notes there is laṅgha (leap); and on four, sañcāra (movement).

commentary.text: Just as in a field of work one person alone can do only a little work, two people together more than that, three together more than that, and four people together accomplish many kinds of tasks — in the same way, making clear which elements grow, when [notes] are used in rāgas, from one note up to four notes, the śloka above has told that as long as any note stays alone, no action other than kampana (shake) can happen in it, as if that note were trembling, frightened of loneliness. But as soon as it meets one other note, many activities begin between the two of them: ādisparśa (touch at the beginning), antasparśa (touch at the end), turning back and forth, and so on. Seen in a worldly way, it seems as if the two have become so absorbed in each other that a third note will have to come to bring them to their senses.

Now when the third also comes and joins, then among those three notes, besides the earlier actions, a new action in the form of laṅghana (leaping) begins, as if the third were now and then making a disturbance between the two notes. After that, when four notes come together, along with the growth of the earlier actions a new action, saṃvāda (dialogue), begins, as if all could become calm and happy. The gradation of qualities grows only up to four notes, so in practice the sargam is what is well known. The actions of different notes among the notes, which come from the mixing of the qualities written above, have been given the name varṇa. So it is from the actions that the varṇa, that is, the class (jāti), is decided.
